To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of cores needed to achieve the maximum cancer detection is 10, and the number of cores that achieves a 95% probability of cancer detection is 14, for patients undergoing MRI-ultrasound fusion biopsy.

the minimum number of cores required to detect a prostate cancer is 6, and that the minimum number required to detect a clinically significant cancer is 12, with the probability of missing a clinically significant cancer being less than 10% for 12 and less than 5% for 14.

the minimum number of MRI-ultrasound targeted cores needed to detect clinically significant prostate cancer (Gleason score 3+4, 4+3, 4+4 or ≥5) was 3 and the minimum number needed to detect clinically insignificant prostate cancer (Glyleason score ≤3+3) was 2.

a 12-core prostate biopsy protocol can detect prostate cancer with a similar accuracy to a 14- or 16-core protocol, and that the number of cancer-positive cores is not a good predictor of prostate cancer volume.
